title: Trump Says Deportation Policy Was 'Too Tough' in Post-Midterm Interview
excerpt: In his first sit-down since the Republican midterm defeat, President Trump told 60 Minutes removals of workers with good jobs hurt his party — an hour after recording, he replaced his chief of staff with the policy's architect, Stephen Miller.
body:
• President Donald Trump told CBS's 60 Minutes that his deportation policy was "too tough" — "I think it might be too tough" — in an interview recorded at the White House on Friday and aired Sunday, November 8, according to The Hindu.
  • Trump said the policy both helped and hurt in the midterms: high marks for closing the border and removing criminals, but removals of people with good jobs whose only violation was entering illegally cost his party.
  • About an hour after the interview, Trump replaced chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the architect of the deportation policy — a move in the opposite direction from the interview's tone.
  • For readers in the immigration system: nothing in the interview changes a rule, a fee, a deadline or a pending case. Trump said he would "love to do something on immigration" with the incoming Democratic Congress, which is a stated wish, not a bill.

US President Donald Trump has said his mass deportation policy was "too tough," in his first major interview since the Republican Party's heavy defeat in last Tuesday's midterm elections. Asked by 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat whether the deportation policy went too far, Trump replied, "I think it was too tough... I think it might be too tough."

"I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs."

— President Donald Trump, 60 Minutes

Who is affected — and what has actually changed

The remarks concern the administration's removal policy toward undocumented immigrants, including long-settled workers. Trump drew the line himself in the interview, as reported in the 60 Minutes transcript: enforcement against "the killers," "the rough ones" and "the drug dealers" was, in his account, a political strength; removing people whose single violation was illegal entry, and who held jobs, was where it hurt. No executive order, regulation or enforcement guidance accompanied the interview. Anyone with a pending removal case, a work-authorisation renewal or a family petition is in exactly the position they were in last week.

The personnel move that points the other way

The complication arrived within hours of the recording. CBS noted, and Sweden Herald's account of the interview also reported, that on Friday Trump replaced his chief of staff, Susie Wiles, with Stephen Miller — the official most closely identified with designing the deportation policy the president was describing as too tough. That appointment raised concerns, Sweden Herald reported, that policy toward undocumented migrants could become tougher still, whatever the interview suggested.

What happens next

Trump told Douthat he would "love to do something on immigration" with the incoming Democratic Congress. Any such deal would need legislation, and none has been introduced on the basis of the interview. For now, readers should treat the remarks as a political signal after an election defeat — notable because the president rarely criticises his own signature policy — and watch two concrete things: whether Miller's arrival produces new enforcement guidance, and whether any immigration bill actually reaches Congress. Until one of those happens, the rules have not moved.
